name: Seed oil avoidance

lead: Seed oil avoidance means removing refined vegetable oils such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn and safflower and cooking with fats like butter, tallow or olive oil. People do it for clearer skin, less puffiness and a leaner look, which they link to lower inflammation.

Proponents point to omega-6 linoleic acid, a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio and industrial solvent extraction. Nutrition reviews report that linoleic acid does not reliably raise inflammatory markers and that swapping saturated for unsaturated fat is linked to better cardiovascular markers. No studies have tested seed oil avoidance for skin or facial appearance.

paras: Followers read labels, cook at home and swap oils for butter, tallow, ghee or olive oil, and often pair it with carnivore or primal eating or other clean-eating habits. Restaurants and packaged foods are the hard part, since seed oils are widely used. Users report judging results over several weeks.

Avoiding seed oils is not itself documented as harmful, but reviews note that shifting toward saturated fat could raise LDL cholesterol. Health bodies generally continue to recommend unsaturated oils over saturated fats. Strict avoidance can make eating out difficult.

angle.text: Followers cut canola, soybean, sunflower and similar oils expecting lower inflammation, clearer skin and less puffiness. It is bundled with other clean-eating habits in looksmaxxing forums; nutrition reviews generally report that these oils do not reliably raise inflammation markers.

lead: Seed oil avoidance is a dietary practice in which people exclude refined oils pressed or solvent-extracted from seeds, such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn, cottonseed, safflower, grapeseed and rice bran, often called the 'hateful eight' in online discussion.[1] Adherents say the oils drive inflammation, skin problems and chronic disease; in looksmaxxing forums it is bundled with other 'clean' eating ideas.[2][3]

Reviews of human evidence report that linoleic acid, the main omega-6 fat in these oils, does not reliably raise inflammatory markers, and that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is linked to better cardiovascular risk markers.[1][4][5] A 2025 narrative review describes the campaign against seed oils as contrary to dietary guidelines and available human research.[4] No clinical studies were found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or facial appearance.
infobox: Canola, soybean, sunflower, corn, cottonseed, safflower, grapeseed, rice bran oils
Around 2018 to 2020 via podcasts and social media
Butter, beef tallow, olive oil, coconut oil

paras: Seed oils are fats obtained from the seeds of plants and used for cooking, packaged foods and, in other forms, topical products.[6] Critics of the oils usually target eight refined oils, a grouping popularised by physician Cate Shanahan on a podcast in 2020.[1]
Practitioners avoid them in home cooking and restaurants, sometimes consulting lists of restaurants said to cook with butter or tallow.[7]

According to Wikipedia, a movement claiming that refined vegetable oils drive chronic disease circulated online from about 2018 and gained wide attention in 2020 after podcaster Joe Rogan interviewed carnivore-diet promoter Paul Saladino.[1] Wikipedia also records that opposition to seed oils later entered US political discussion, including statements by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in 2024 and 2025.[1]
In looksmaxxing forums the topic appears in jokes and serious threads, including a satirical 'seed oils will ascend you' post and practical threads about which fast-food chains avoid them.[2][7]

Proponents argue that industrial processing with solvents such as hexane, high omega-6 linoleic acid content and a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio promote inflammation and disease, and they extend this to skin and appearance.[1][2] Some forum members suggest taking krill oil to rebalance omega-3 when eating out; others reply that cooking at home with olive oil or butter is sufficient.[3]

A 2025 narrative review in Nutrition Reviews concluded that the human evidence does not support the claim that seed oils drive cardiometabolic disease and noted that saturated fat is linked to higher LDL cholesterol.[4] A 2025 systematic review examined seed-oil effects on lipid profile, inflammatory and oxidative markers and glycemic control in diabetic and dyslipidemic patients.[8]

A randomized trial in overweight and obese adults found no evidence of differing effects between sunflower and rapeseed oil on coronary artery disease and chronic kidney disease biomarkers.[9] A review of the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio in Missouri Medicine argued that a lower ratio may reduce autoimmune, asthma and allergy risk, a position cited by some proponents.[10]

Wikipedia reports that the World Cancer Research Fund and Cancer Council Australia have stated there is no evidence seed oils raise cancer risk, and that the US FDA considers consumer vegetable oils generally recognized as safe.[1]

Research on seed oils for skin mostly concerns topical use rather than dietary avoidance. A review of African plant oils in dermatology describes traditional topical uses, with potential benefits and adverse effects.[6] These findings do not address whether eating seed oils changes skin appearance.

No studies found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or appearance. Related human research on dietary seed oils examines cardiometabolic markers, including a randomized trial of sunflower versus rapeseed oil and systematic reviews of lipid and inflammatory outcomes.[8][9]

lore.intro: Seed oil avoidance appears on looksmax.org as a health and skin theory, a joke ('seed oils will ascend you'), and a practical question of how to eat out without them.[2][7][3]
